name: Madras plaid shirt

card.summary: A lightweight, brightly checked cotton shirt from the preppy tradition that adds color and a relaxed, put-together summer look.

quick.overview:
The madras plaid shirt is a short- or long-sleeved button-up made from handwoven-style cotton in a multicolored check. It is a staple of preppy and Ivy summer dressing, and people wear it to look relaxed, colorful and deliberately dressed in warm weather.

The cloth is named after Madras (now Chennai) in India. It reached American style in the twentieth century and became widely popular in the 1960s. Style writers and brands describe it as a seasonal, casual alternative to the plain Oxford shirt.
quick.how: It is typically worn untucked or tucked with chinos, shorts or white trousers, with loafers, boat shoes or clean sneakers. Wearers usually pick one plaid with muted tones for versatility, and keep the rest of the outfit plain so the pattern is the focus.
quick.risks: Traditional madras was dyed so that colors bleed and fade when washed, and the care advice for authentic cloth is gentle, cold washing. Bold plaids can clash with other patterns.

lead: A madras plaid shirt is a lightweight cotton shirt woven in a bright, irregular plaid, historically linked to the preppy style of the American Northeast. For appearance it provides color, texture and a casual-smart summer look that stands out from solid shirts.[1]

Madras fabric is named for Madras, now Chennai, in Tamil Nadu, India. Authentic madras is described as handwoven, with the same pattern on both faces and a slightly uneven, slubbed texture from carded short-staple cotton.[1] Madras cloth reached the US early; a gift of it to the Collegiate School of Connecticut, later Yale, is dated to 1718.[1]

The shirt became popular in the 1960s among baby boomers adopting preppy dress.[1] Seersucker and madras are among the fabrics commonly used for summer sport jackets and Bermuda shorts in preppy and Ivy style.[2]

angle.text: The shirt changes the look of an outfit directly through color and pattern. Its breathable cotton also suits hot weather, which people use to look polished without wearing heavy layers.

paras: The shirt is made from madras cotton, a lightweight cloth whose plaid resembles tartan but uses brighter, more irregular color combinations. Authentic cloth is handwoven and comes from a carded short-staple cotton that gives it visible slubs.[1]

Dutch and British traders reached the Madras region in the seventeenth century, and the English East India Company established a trading post there in the mid-1600s, attracting weaving families.[1] The name is credited to shirtmaker David J. Anderson in 1844, although the cloth was called that earlier, and Sears offered a madras shirt in its 1897 catalog.[1]

In the 1930s, madras clothing is described as a status symbol in the US because only wealthy Americans could afford Caribbean vacations during the Depression.[1] In 1958 importer William Jacobson bought madras from exporter Captain C.P. Krishnan, and Brooks Brothers purchased 10,000 yards. The garments faded in the wash because the care advice had not reached the retailer, and advertiser David Ogilvy turned this into a selling point with the phrase "guaranteed to bleed."[1]

Preppy fashion grew out of the early-twentieth-century Ivy style and is associated with brands such as Brooks Brothers, J. Press and Ralph Lauren.[2] Madras appears alongside seersucker in summer sport jackets and Bermuda shorts, and Lisa Birnbach's 1980 book The Official Preppy Handbook helped revive the style.[2]

timeline.event: Cotton madras is donated to the Collegiate School of Connecticut, later Yale.[1]
Sears lists a madras shirt in its catalog.[1]
Brooks Brothers buys 10,000 yards of bleeding madras; Ogilvy markets it as "guaranteed to bleed."[1]
Plaid madras shirts become popular among preppy-dressing baby boomers.[1]
The Official Preppy Handbook revives interest in preppy dress.[2]
